newsitem.title: USA: Bermuda exchange wins SEC offshore designation.
newsitem.headline: Bermuda exchange wins SEC offshore designation.

text.p: The Bermuda Stock Exchange's aggressive growth plan took another jump forward on Monday, when the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission designated the exchange as a U.S.-recognized offshore securities market, the head of the exchange told Reuters.

"We feel it's a very important milestone in the transformation of the exchange from a purely domestic market into the world's first truly offshore securities exchange," exchange chief executive officer William Woods said in a telephone interview from Hamilton, Bermuda.

"It shows that we have a credible track record according to SEC standards. We think it will definitely encourage U.S. investment houses to seriously think of taking a trading membership on our exchange now," he added.

The Bermuda Stock Exchange ended 1995 with market capitalization of just over $1 billion, but its growth has soared since then. At the end of September, Woods said the exchange had market capitalization of more than $25 billion.
"We're growing quickly and a number of international companies have taken listings here.
"Some are Bermuda-based reinsurance specialists like ACE Ltd and EXEL Ltd," he said.
The exchange aims to end 1997 with market capatalization of "over the $30 billion mark," he said.

The new SEC designation of the exchange as an "offshore securities market" within the meaning of Rule 902(a) of Regulation S means that Bermuda can offer cross-trading of stocks outside of New York trading hours, Woods said. New York Stock Exchange-listed securities are allowed some cross-trading outside regular hours on offshore stock exchanges.

"Traditionally, U.S. houses have performed this cross-trading in London. But we offer a number of advantages, including the time zone because we're one hour ahead of New York. And we have a cost advantage because we've set our crossing fee at 50 cents per trade with a maximum of $50 per trade for a basket of stocks," he said.
The Bermuda exchange is also trying to position itself as a competitor to the Luxembourg exchange for the listing of Latin American and Eurobond issues, he said.

"We think it becomes attractive for Latin American issuers because we're closer to the United States. In terms of time zone, these deals are often driven out of New York and it's easier for bankers to deal with Bermuda rather than Luxembourg, which is six hours ahead."
The Bermuda exchange currently lists 50 equity issues, 60 investment funds and nine debt issues.
